1	# Eric's method baseline (draft for Eric's review)
2	
3	Purpose: this is the step-1 baseline for Flint. It pulls every position, practice, and decision rule out of Eric's own 23-document corpus (Baylor Applied Performance playbook, protocols, assessment manual, professional writing, and HHPR 5355 graduate-course material) so that every future synthesis note comparing an outside source (Landon Evans, TB's Training Info, Old Bull, Harries RTP, SCN/Moyer, etc.) has something of Eric's own to compare against. Date: 2026-09-26.
4	
5	## Provenance note (read this before the bullets)
6	
7	Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:
8	
9	- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).
10	- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
11	- **Both class transcripts (Class 1, Class 3) are diarized entirely under one Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line, across 100+ minutes combined.** This is true even for Class 3 (Feb. 5), which the syllabus assigns solo to Rash. Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident, first-person claim in the text. Flint should treat these as "the HHPR 5355 teaching team's shared position, individual speaker unconfirmed" until Eric ratifies them.
12	  - **Confirmed by Eric, 2026-09-26:** HHPR 5355 is taught each spring by Chris Ruf, Eric and Mike Wenger. The lecture material is split among the three of them. This confirms the course is partly Eric's, but it cannot say who spoke a given transcript line. So transcript bullets stay tagged Inferred and read as **course team positions**. Each one becomes Eric's own only when he claims it, in review or in the interview.
13	- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.
14	
15	Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).
16	
17	---
18	
19	## Philosophy and decision principles
20	
21	- Applied Performance's stated mission is to "drive elite performance ... by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships," enabling the high-performance team to answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones — not to hand down answers unilaterally. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
22	- The department's four operating principles are Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance, Performance Team Collaboration, and Research and Development. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
23	- Institutional framing: "Prepare Champions for Life" across four pillars (academic, athletic, social, spiritual), operationalized through six "One Standard, One Accord" principles. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.3-4]
24	- Data collection is judged on cost versus insight: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
25	- A test can be scientifically valid and still be the wrong choice operationally: "The lesson wasn't about the test. It was about the infrastructure required to make a test useful ... even a valid test stops being valuable" without staff ownership and consistent collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
26	- "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" — a test's validity doesn't rescue it if it can't be collected consistently at scale. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
27	- Reject ownership language ("my team," "my athletes"): the athlete's development is shared across every department that touches them, not owned by any one coach. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5, "we got to get away from like the me and my"]
28	- Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, through sound programming, progression, and collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to promise injury prevention. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4]
29	- Be skeptical of social-media-driven training trends: a viral clip is "just a brief snapshot," stripped of the context that would tell you whether it's sound. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.3]
30	- Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery." **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
31	- "Knowledge from experience" as a stated operating value: safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5; week1-lecture.md p.12]
32	
33	## Department model and roles
34	
35	- Applied Performance operates inside the Baylor Athletics Health & Wellness department, alongside (not above or below) Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.5-6]
36	- The athlete is described as the hub of a wheel, with every support function (academics, Athletic Medicine, nutrition, mental health, Applied Performance) as a spoke — no single discipline owns the athlete's development. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
37	- An Athletic Performance coach is framed in explicit contrast to a narrower "Strength Coach" identity: "we/our" and holistic mind-body-spirit development versus "me/my" and just lifting/running. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5; week1-lecture.md p.13]
38	- The current Baylor Applied Performance Operations Guide is judged, by Eric's own gap analysis, as missing: an intern/GA curriculum, sport-specific data dictionaries, daily operational checklists, Baylor-specific (not generic-template) technology workflows, and a guiding-principles/policy framework for staff and interns. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 1, 3.2]
39	- A three-phase roadmap (Foundation, weeks 1-4; Operational Depth, weeks 5-10; Education and Culture, weeks 11-16+) is the stated plan to close those gaps, ending with an annual Playbook review cycle each May. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
40	- Some assessments coaches already run inside practice should not be duplicated; use that existing data to triangulate rather than re-testing, and set objective criteria for coach-mandated tests when none exist. **Inferred (author uncertain — see Testing tensions)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Team Cultures and Assessments"]
41	
42	## Testing and assessment
43	
44	- Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
45	- Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6]
46	- Favor a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories over an exhaustive battery — illustrated with a simple baseball profile (bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max). **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6; week1-lecture.md p.16]
47	- Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
48	- Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) — both are tracked, but they answer different questions. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
49	- Reassessment timing is governed by three factors: proximity to competition, the expected magnitude of change for that training phase and athlete level, and current recovery status — "do not reassess an athlete if there is known fatigue." **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Reassessment"]
50	- 1RM testing is reserved for intermediate/advanced athletes with real exposure to near-maximal loads; novices and most women's-sport testing default to repetition-max protocols, which are described as better tolerated neurologically, psychologically, and physically for smaller-framed lifters. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
51	- Velocity-based 1RM estimation (linear-displacement transducer, ~10% load increments to 85-90% or a target mean velocity) is preferred over live 1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing, with published target mean velocities at 1RM (squat 0.3 m/s, bench 0.2 m/s, power hang snatch 1.0 m/s, power hang clean 0.8 m/s). **Inferred (author uncertain — legacy protocol, see Tensions)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
52	- The Baylor Sport Assessment Table (V4) assigns a specific battery per sport (movement screen, anthropometrics, CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower strength estimation, strength endurance, aerobic fitness, repeat sprint ability, linear sprint, change of direction) rather than testing every sport the same way. **Inferred** [update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md]
53	- The current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as a real usability problem for staff and a priority to fix with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized dictionaries. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]
54	
55	## Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring
56	
57	- Force plates (CMJ testing) were already the department's longitudinal performance-tracking tool well before the 2022-23 wellness-survey experiment, and remained in place after that experiment ended. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
58	- Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
59	- The standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks: hands-free squat, squat jump (quarter-squat start, 3s hold), countermovement jump (x3), hop test / repeated CMJ (10 reps total, n=5 pairs), and single-leg CMJ (x3 per leg) — each with a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol. **Inferred (protocol; author uncertain)** [revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
60	- The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps. **Inferred (protocol)** [protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md; revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
61	- Metric selection for force-plate reporting follows a disciplined framework: pick 1-2 output metrics (the obvious performance result, e.g. jump height), 1-3 driver metrics (what produces the output, e.g. braking/propulsive force), 1-3 strategy metrics (how the athlete achieved it, e.g. phase durations), optional symmetry metrics (L/R differences), and add "fluffy" metrics (peak power, average power, RFD) only with a specific, defensible rationale. **Adopted practice, framework not Eric's own** [hd-odsf-metrics.md — origin: Hawkin Dynamics]
62	- NordBord hamstring testing was retired for roster-wide football monitoring (after starting January 2023) because a 25-30 minute per-group session could not be sustained across 120+ athletes without large, uncontrolled gaps in the data, and staff turnover ended the coordination needed to run it at scale. The decision rule stated: keep a demanding test only where you have "smaller numbers, clear clinical purpose, dedicated oversight" (now used for targeted return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing); drop it where you can't guarantee consistent, comparable collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
63	
64	## Load monitoring and GPS
65	
66	- The core GPS technology stack is Catapult (device/OpenField software) with Kitman Labs as the central athlete-management system for cross-technology storage, scaling, and visualization. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
67	- Core GPS metrics tracked: maximum velocity, total distance, player load, field time, heart-rate bands, velocity/acceleration/deceleration effort bands, and Inertial Movement Analysis (IMA) for indoor sessions without GPS coverage. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.11-13, Data Dictionary]
68	- A documented step-by-step SOP exists for the full GPS session lifecycle: charging, alarm-setting, activity creation, live period management, post-session sync, data cleaning (spike detection), tagging, and PDF export/reporting. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.9-11]
69	- No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist in the documented data dictionary — it is generic and vendor-organized, and building contextualized per-sport thresholds is named as unfinished, prioritized work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a gap)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]
70	- Heavy GPS/load-monitoring data was described as having bred a "culture of fear" in the field broadly (do less, to protect recovery), which the course material argues actually leaves athletes under-prepared for competition. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
71	- Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal. Wellness surveys are still used, deliberately, in return-to-play scenarios and with athletes managing chronic health conditions, where subjective context still adds value objective data can't supply. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
72	
73	## Speed and sprint
74	
75	- Linear sprint testing uses a 2-point start for team-sport athletes (for reliability), athlete self-selected start timing, at least two maximal-effort reps over 30-40 meters. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
76	- Split times are interpreted by physical quality, not just total time: 0-10m is read as an acceleration score (reflecting maximal strength/power/slow stretch-shortening-cycle development), 30-40m as a speed score (reflecting sprint-specific/fast stretch-shortening-cycle development), and 40m peak velocity is derived from the 30-40m split divided by 10. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
77	- SmartSpeed timing gates are the standard tool for sprint, agility, and reaction-time testing across the department. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
78	- Speed is taught as the quality with the shortest ground-contact-time demand (~0.08s male, ~0.10s female at max velocity) and is described as harder to train and more genetically constrained than strength or power, but as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.11]
79	
80	## Strength and power
81	
82	- The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass." **Inferred (transcript + shared course material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10; week1-lecture.md pp.23,26]
83	- Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific." **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16; week1-lecture.md pp.32-36]
84	- The Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production, and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14; week1-lecture.md p.34]
85	- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
86	- Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + shared slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21]
87	- Undulating/non-linear periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression, specifically to avoid staleness while still building tolerance for higher loads. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed but first-person: "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use")** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26]
88	- Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block, used consistently across strength and power teaching. **Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.15]
89	- Strength's residual training effect is treated as roughly 30 days — a minimal retention dose is still trained within that window, even during lower-strength-emphasis blocks. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25]
90	- Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46]
91	
92	## Conditioning and energy systems
93	
94	- Conditioning is defined two ways: (1) how well an athlete can meet the energy requirements of their specific sport/activity, and (2) how well they sustain strength, speed, and power output across a full competition. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.22]
95	- All three energy systems (alactic ~10-12s highest power, glycolytic/anaerobic-lactic ~60-90s medium capacity, aerobic hours-long lowest power/highest capacity) are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.19; class-4-2026.md p.15]
96	- A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once — priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands (e.g., for football: prepared for fall camp first, then the first game). **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31]
97	- For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]

177	## Tensions and contradictions
178	
179	1. **The task's own premise doesn't fully hold.** Both class transcripts (Class 1 and Class 3) are diarized entirely under a single Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line — including Class 3, which the Spring 2026 teaching schedule assigns solo to Rash (`spring-2026-teaching.md`: "Feb. 5 | Conditioning - Alactic-Aerobic | Rash"). Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name instead of doing real per-speaker diarization. This means roughly 30,000 words of the richest, most first-person material in this corpus cannot be confidently attributed to Rash specifically versus Ruf or Wenger. Every transcript-sourced bullet above is marked Inferred for this reason, even where the underlying statement is a confident, first-person claim.
180	
181	2. **Department reporting model is not internally consistent.** The Playbook (p.6) frames Applied Performance as a peer discipline inside Health & Wellness that "enables" Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Nutrition, and Mental Health to answer their own questions. But Week 1 course material lists "Applied Performance" as one of many training sub-categories nested under Athletic Performance itself (p.11), and the same transcript narration describes Rash's role as "helping program and plan the training" — a support-staff framing, not a peer-department framing. Which model actually governs day-to-day authority is not reconciled anywhere in these documents.
182	
183	3. **Coach's-eye-first versus objective-first is argued both ways.** The course material repeatedly argues that "you don't need a fancy test... you have to have a good coach's eye" and criticizes the GPS/load-monitoring era for breeding a fear-driven under-training culture. Eric's own SportSmith writing moves the opposite direction on daily monitoring specifically: he replaced subjective wellness surveys with objective force-plate mRSI because subjective self-report couldn't be trusted. Both share a skepticism of trendy or convenient data, but they land on opposite defaults (trust the trained eye vs. require an objective number) for the daily-monitoring question specifically.
184	
185	4. **The Assessment Manual (V12) reads as an older document than the current technology stack.** It builds its 1RM-estimation protocol around GymAware, and its CMJ description references a "contact mat" for jump height. The current Playbook technology stack and the Development Plan both center velocity-based training on Perch, not GymAware, and the current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol runs all CMJ variants exclusively on ForceDecks force plates, with no contact mat mentioned. This suggests the Assessment Manual predates the current VALD/Perch-centered stack and may be a legacy document rather than the currently operative protocol — worth confirming directly with Eric before treating any of its specifics as current practice.
186	
187	5. **Testing cueing instructions conflict across two protocol documents for the same test.** The Assessment Manual's CMJ instructions say explicitly: "Do not coach the strategy of jumping." The current Force Plate Testing V3 protocol gives testers specific verbal cues to give athletes during CMJ, squat-jump, and hop-test administration ("keep chest up," "land softly," "land stiff-legged on only the toes"). These may be reconcilable (safety/technique cues vs. jump-strategy cues are different things), but the two documents read differently on how much a tester should say out loud.
188	
189	6. **Two different anaerobic-threshold heart-rate methods appear back to back in the same slide deck without being reconciled.** One slide gives an age-based formula (max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at ~85% of that), and the very next slides give a body-size-based table (big/medium/small athlete, ~165/170/175 bpm threshold) as the operational standard used elsewhere throughout the conditioning material. Which one is actually used day to day is not stated. [class-4-2026.md pp.27-29]
190	
191	7. **The Development Plan's own critique cuts against the corpus it's part of.** It states the current Baylor Playbook "has no educational component whatsoever" and reads "like a vendor product reference manual," even though Eric personally co-teaches a full graduate-level course covering much of the same material the Playbook is missing. The department's teaching capacity clearly exists; it just hasn't been captured back into the Playbook or a formal intern curriculum yet.
192	
193	8. **The Playbook's NordBord documentation has not caught up with practice.** The Playbook's Technology Overview and Workflows still document a full, unqualified, roster-style NordBord data-collection SOP. The SportSmith piece describes explicitly retiring roster-wide NordBord testing for football starting after January 2023, keeping it only for small, targeted return-to-play groups. The written SOP has not been updated to reflect that decision.
194	
195	9. **A personally-stated periodization preference is stated inside an unreliable-speaker transcript.** "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use" (about undulating over linear periodization) is a strong, direct, first-person preference claim — but it comes from the same unreliably-diarized Class 1 transcript described in Tension 1, so it cannot be confirmed as Eric's own stated preference without his direct confirmation.
196	
197	10. **Older vs. current unit-goal templates show almost no adopted content.** The Geyer and Skodinski Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are staff-authored templates for individual sport programming philosophy; Geyer's is mostly filled in (periodization model, weekly split, KPI tests for softball), Skodinski's is nearly blank (just the section headers). Neither is attributed to Eric, and there's no equivalent document in this corpus showing Eric's own answers to the same template questions — a real gap if Flint wants Eric's own unit-goal-style programming philosophy in his own words.

## Summary

Phil Wagner, founder of Sparta Science, argues that a standardized vertical jump on a portable force plate can flag injury risk and physical readiness, including upper body injuries in baseball pitchers. He models his approach on medicine: clinical expertise, athlete input and evidence, plus a standardized assessment. The jump is scored on three phases (load, explode, drive) into a "movement signature" with thresholds, and the software turns imbalances into a prioritized exercise plan. He adds injury history, training load and sleep to a dashboard. The talk is a vendor presentation with case studies and claimed results but no published data shown on screen. The Q&A covers balance and landing tests, buy-in, football versus baseball targets and youth use.

## Key claims

- Wagner says a jump can predict an injury, specifically an upper body injury. [01:05]
- He says a company needs years of data to build prediction models, and that Sparta has seven years of data across MLB, NFL, NCAA and several countries. [03:36] [04:07]
- He says the force plate jump was chosen because other tests (sprinting, agility, throwing, hitting, single-leg jumps) are less reliable. [09:05]
- The jump is split into load (standing to squat), explode (leaving the bottom) and drive (how long the movement is prolonged); each is predictive of success for different positions or sports. [09:05] [09:36]
- The three phase scores form a "movement signature," expressed as a t-score where 50 is average. [10:06] [10:39]
- A healthy imbalance, meaning a specific uneven pattern in the signature, is associated in a pitcher case study with success and with ground ball percentage; third parties (Stanford School of Medicine, BYU statistics) are said to have validated it. [11:10]
- A minor league pitcher had a high drive without matching load and then tore his UCL; Wagner says a publication shows drive rising without load predicts severe elbow injury. [12:43] [13:13]
- The plan starts with the lowest variable, then works on the next one if it is far enough from the others, left/right differences, recovery, nutrition, hydration and sleep. [13:45] [14:15]
- Wagner says being digital is not the same as being scientific. [14:51]
- He says the program can tell where an athlete will be in 14 days after a given squat prescription, and that general managers ask how long until risk is reduced. [15:21]
- Previous injury is the biggest predictor of any injury, and recent sport load (pitch count over 30 days above two standard deviations) adds risk. [16:24] [16:54]
- He claims organizations can decrease injuries 10 to 20% each year. [17:24]
- Sleep is entered subjectively by athletes on a phone app, and he says entries can vary when contracts are guaranteed or not. [19:52]
- Sparta describes itself as a database company, not a force plate company, and sees other biomarkers as future additions. [20:23]
- A left versus right balance test (eyes closed is more reliable) and a single-leg landing test are used for return to play when jumping is not possible. [21:29] [22:31]
- Prior injury is added as a covariate in the predictive model, with decision trees run by statistics partners. [24:05] [24:37]
- The test is physical and removes skill, so it is meant to show whether more skill work or more physical work is needed. [26:42] [27:12]
- Exercises can push a variable the wrong way; squat has the largest effect on load and is the biggest negative detractor of drive. [28:16] [28:49]
- Position affects load, but movement patterns are shared by skill type across sports (for example point guards resemble defensive backs). [29:20]
- The software does not replace conversations with the athlete; a subjective flag should prompt a discussion. [29:52] [30:23]
- Organizations that are most transparent, for example athletes reviewing their data within 24 hours, see more buy-in. [31:40]
- He says athletes are not blind to the test, averages are used, and only the load variable shows a learning effect, which can expose pain or soreness. [32:19] [32:50]
- In baseball the largest prediction target is Tommy John UCL injury (four years of weekly MLB assessments); in the NFL it is a foot injury (caption "Liz Frank," probably Lisfranc, caption spelling), then ACL. [34:05] [34:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- "Predict 99 injuries" for an MLB team in 2014 [04:07]. Captions may have garbled this figure; the text reads "99 injuries" with no denominator or percentage. Not usable as stated.
- "$22.5 million" then "$225 million" of predicted savings for a season [04:39]. The two figures conflict in the captions; I cannot tell which is right.
- MLB losses to injury over $700 million in 2014 [05:12].
- Seven years of data [03:36]. Models take 3 to 5 years to build [04:07].
- Force plate weighs about 40 pounds and is portable [08:33].
- T-score: a scaled percentile where 50 is average [10:06] [10:39].
- Drive "more than 15 from the others" is the flag for severe elbow injury [13:13]. The captions read "more than 15," with no unit, so the unit is unverified. The second-variable flag is "more than five" [13:45].
- 80% of bodyweight for five sets of five leads to a known state at 14 days [15:21].
- Pitch count in the last 30 days more than two standard deviations above the athlete's normal [16:54].
- Claimed injury reduction of 10 to 20% per year [17:24].
- Balance test: 20 seconds, two trials each side; left/right t-score 48 to 51 is typical, below 40 is a large risk increase, a left/right difference of 10 is a large injury increase [21:29] [23:04].
- Test duration context: 30 minute session including Q&A was announced [00:32].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Vertical jump on a portable force plate with a standardized warm-up and set number of trials. [07:48]
- Three phase scores (load, explode, drive) into a movement signature and t-scores. [09:36] [10:06]
- Thresholds for what is meaningful, built from aggregated, anonymous data of high school, college and professional athletes. [04:07] [10:39] [25:07]
- Prioritized prescription: address lowest variable first, then next if far from the others, then left/right and recovery inputs. [13:45]
- Dashboard combining scan, previous injury, sport load and recovery logs, with alerts. [16:24] [17:56]
- Decision trees with covariates, run by statistics partners. [24:37]
- Medicine analogy: clinical expertise, patient input, evidence. [05:43] [06:13]

## Limits and open questions

- No data, sample sizes, false positive rates or confidence intervals are shown in the captions. "Predict" is used without saying prospective or retrospective.
- The 99 injuries and savings figures are garbled or inconsistent in the captions.
- The publication on drive and elbow injury is not named [12:43].
- Claimed third-party validation (Stanford, BYU) is stated without results [11:10].
- The 10 to 20% yearly injury reduction has no stated comparison group [17:24].
- Commercial view: the speaker founded and sells the product.
- The 14-day claim is stated as known, with no evidence given [15:21].
- The speaker says the jump predicts upper body injury, yet the main case is one pitcher, plus one relief case of an improved pitcher.
- Sleep is self-reported, and the speaker notes that reports may vary with contract status [19:52].
- Football findings are described as a ground-up model, so less mature than baseball [34:35].

## Q&A

- How is sleep monitored? Subjective phone entry. [19:52]
- Would other body chemistry data be added? Yes, as a future area. [20:23]
- Left versus right balance test: how does it work? Shown with a return-to-play example. [21:29]
- How are covariates like existing injury handled? Added to the model. [24:37]
- Can this apply to youth? Not yet, database is high school and up. [25:07]
- Individual sports? Mostly track and field so far, plus NBA and Kansas basketball. [25:37]
- In-game wearables and skill versus physical? The test removes skill. [26:42]
- Negative effects of exercises? Squat raises load but lowers drive. [28:16]
- Positions? Loading differs, movement is shared by skill type. [29:20]
- Subjective variables? Not correlated yet. [29:52]
- Player buy-in? Transparency, such as reviewing data within 24 hours. [31:09]
- Is the test blind and can it be cheated? Not blind; averaged; load is sensitive to pain. [32:19]
- Future of Sparta? Help organizations prioritize time. [33:35]
- What do you predict in each sport? UCL in baseball; foot then ACL in the NFL. [34:05]

=== FILE: videos/2016-04-07_Alj_VvBZaqo_can-you-really-predict-athletic-injury-and-performance/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: Alj_VvBZaqo
title: "SSAC16: Can you Really Predict Athletic Injury and Performance?"
event: SSAC16 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Phil Wagner (founder and CEO of Sparta Science, per the host and his own introduction; the host's caption spelling is "Dr phel Wagner")]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, other-sport:baseball, american-football, basketball, competitive-advantage]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Phil Wagner, founder of Sparta Science, argues that a standardized vertical jump on a portable force plate can flag injury risk and physical readiness, including upper body injuries in baseball pitchers. He models the approach on medicine: clinical expertise, athlete input and evidence, plus a standardized assessment. The jump is scored on three phases (load, explode, drive) into a "movement signature" with thresholds, and software turns imbalances into a prioritized exercise plan. Injury history, sport load and sleep sit on a dashboard. The talk is a vendor presentation with case studies and claimed results, but no data tables appear in the captions. The Q&A covers balance and landing tests, buy-in, football versus baseball targets and youth use.

## Key claims

- A jump can predict an injury, specifically an upper body injury. [01:05]
- Building prediction models generally takes 3 to 5 years of data, and Sparta has about seven years across MLB, NFL, NCAA and several countries. [03:36] [04:07]
- The jump was chosen because other tests (sprinting, agility, throwing, hitting, single-leg jumps) are less reliable. [09:05]
- The jump is split into load (standing to squat), explode (how quickly the athlete comes out of the bottom) and drive (how well the movement is prolonged); each is tied to success in different positions or sports. [09:05] [09:36]
- The three scores form a "movement signature," expressed as a t-score where 50 is average. [10:06] [10:39]
- Plates and vertical jumps are not new; what is new is thresholds for what is meaningful. [10:39]
- In one pitcher case, a particular uneven pattern (a "healthy imbalance") is associated with ground ball percentage, and Stanford School of Medicine and BYU statistics are said to have validated it. [11:10]
- A minor league pitcher had rising drive without matching load and then tore his UCL; a publication is said to show drive rising without load predicts severe elbow injury. [12:43] [13:13]
- The plan starts with the lowest variable, then the next one if it is far enough from the others, then left/right differences, recovery, nutrition, hydration and sleep. [13:45] [14:15]
- Being digital is not the same as being scientific. [14:51]
- The program knows where an athlete will be 14 days after a given squat prescription, and general managers call to ask how long until risk is reduced. [15:21]
- Previous injury is the biggest predictor of any injury, and recent sport load adds risk. [16:24] [16:54]
- Organizations can decrease injuries 10 to 20% each year. [17:24]
- Sleep is entered subjectively on a phone app, and the speaker says entries can vary depending on whether contracts are guaranteed. [19:52]
- Sparta is a database company, not a force plate company; other biomarkers are a future area. [20:23]
- A left versus right balance test (eyes closed is more reliable) and a single-leg landing test serve return to play when jumping is not possible. [21:29] [22:31]
- Prior injury is added as a covariate in the predictive model, with decision trees run by statistics partners. [24:05] [24:37]
- The test is physical and removes skill, so it shows whether an athlete needs more skill work or more physical work. [26:42] [27:12]
- Exercises can push a variable the wrong way: squat has the largest effect on load and is the biggest negative detractor of drive. [28:16] [28:49]
- Position affects loading, but movement patterns are shared by skill type across sports. [29:20]
- The system cannot replace discussion; a subjective flag should prompt a conversation with the athlete. [29:52] [30:23]
- Organizations that are most transparent, for example athletes reviewing data within 24 hours, see more buy-in. [31:40]
- The test is not blind; variables are averaged across trials; only load shows a learning effect, which can expose pain or soreness. [32:19] [32:50]
- In baseball the largest prediction target is Tommy John UCL injury (four years of weekly MLB assessments); in the NFL it is a foot injury (caption "Liz Frank," probably Lisfranc, caption spelling), then ACL. [34:05] [34:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- "Predict 99 injuries" for an MLB team in 2014 [04:07]. The captions give no denominator or percentage and may be garbled. Not usable as stated.
- "$22.5 million" then "$225 million" of predicted season savings [04:39]. The two figures conflict in the captions; I cannot tell which is correct.
- MLB lost over $700 million to injury in 2014. [05:12]
- Seven years of data [03:36]; 3 to 5 years to build prediction models [04:07].
- Portable force plate weighing about 40 pounds. [08:33]
- T-score: a scaled, more accurate percentile; 50 is average. [10:06] [10:39]
- Drive "more than 15 from the others" is the flag tied to severe elbow injury [13:13]; the captions give no unit. The second-variable check is "more than five" [13:45]; the following words ("only one way") are garbled.
- Squat at 80% of bodyweight for five sets of five leads to a known state at 14 days. [15:21]
- Pitch count over the last 30 days more than two standard deviations above the athlete's normal. [16:54]
- Claimed injury reduction of 10 to 20% per year. [17:24]
- Balance test: 20 seconds, two on each side; left/right t-score of 48 to 51 shown as typical, below 40 is a large risk increase, a left/right difference of 10 is a large injury increase. [21:29] [23:04]
- Four years of weekly MLB assessments. [34:35]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Vertical jump on a portable force plate with a standardized warm-up and set number of trials. [07:48]
- Load, explode and drive scores combined into a movement signature and t-scores. [09:36] [10:06]
- Thresholds built from an anonymous aggregated database of high school, college and professional athletes. [04:07] [10:39] [25:07]
- Prioritized prescription: lowest variable first, then the next if far from the others, then left/right and recovery inputs. [13:45]
- Dashboard combining scan, previous injury, sport load and recovery logs with alerts. [16:24] [17:56]
- Decision trees with covariates run by statistics partners. [24:37]
- Medicine analogy: clinical expertise, patient input, medically based studies. [05:43] [06:13] [06:44]

## Limits and open questions

- No data, sample sizes, false positive rates or confidence intervals appear in the captions. "Predict" is used without saying whether prospective or retrospective.
- The 99 injuries and savings figures are garbled or inconsistent.
- The publication on drive and elbow injury is not named. [12:43]
- Third-party validation (Stanford, BYU) is stated without results. [11:10]
- The 10 to 20% yearly reduction has no stated comparison group. [17:24]
- The 14-day claim is stated as known with no evidence. [15:21]
- Commercial view: the speaker founded and sells the product.
- The main case studies are two pitchers, one named.
- Sleep is self-reported. [19:52]
- Football prediction is described as a ground-up model, less mature than baseball. [34:35]
- The video has a gap between [17:56] and [18:48], and questions are not audible in the captions, so question wording below is inferred from the answers.

## Q&A

- How is sleep monitored? Subjective phone entry. [19:52]
- Would other body chemistry data be added? Yes, as a future area. [20:23]
- How does the left versus right balance test work? Shown with a return-to-play example. [21:29]
- How are covariates such as existing injury handled? Added to the model. [24:37]
- Can this apply to youth? Not yet; the database starts at high school. [25:07]
- Individual sports? Mostly track and field so far, plus NBA and Kansas basketball. [25:37]
- In-game wearables, skill versus physical? The test removes skill. [26:42]
- Negative effects of exercises? Squat raises load but lowers drive. [28:16]
- Positions? Loading differs; movement is shared by skill type. [29:20]
- Subjective variables? Not correlated yet; they should prompt a discussion. [29:52]
- Player buy-in? Transparency, such as reviewing data within 24 hours. [31:09]
- Is the test blind, can it be cheated? Not blind; averaged; load is sensitive to pain. [32:19]
- Future of Sparta? Help organizations prioritize their time. [33:35]
- What is predicted in each sport? UCL in baseball; foot then ACL in the NFL. [34:05]

=== FILE: videos/2016-04-07_Alj_VvBZaqo_can-you-really-predict-athletic-injury-and-performance/applications.md ===
---
type: video-applications
video_id: Alj_VvBZaqo
status: draft
---

## Where this applies

- Inference: Map the talk's load, explode and drive phases onto the driver and strategy metrics Applied Performance already reads from ForceDecks countermovement jumps (for example braking and propulsive phase metrics and phase durations), and check whether any phase-imbalance pattern separates football position groups.
- Inference: Use a single-leg landing and balance benchmark, compared with each athlete's own preseason baseline, as one late-stage return-to-play data point shared with Athletic Medicine.
- Inference: Flag a GPS session or four-week block when an athlete's load sits more than two standard deviations above his own rolling baseline, as a prompt for a conversation, not an automatic restriction.
- Inference: Record prior injury history as a covariate whenever a force plate or GPS flag is reviewed, since the speaker calls previous injury the biggest predictor.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ testing was chosen as the readiness marker because it is objective, consistent and actionable, and wellness surveys were dropped because athletes learned to game them. The talk agrees on the force plate as the core tool and on the weakness of self-reported sleep (the speaker says entries vary with contract status [19:52]).
- Eric's baseline: metric selection follows output, driver and strategy metrics (Hawkin Dynamics' framework). The talk extends this with a three-phase signature but gives no sample to show it beats that approach.
- Eric's baseline: testing must be repeatable ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April"). The talk agrees: it standardized warm-up and number of trials. [07:48]
- Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, and no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric; no sport-specific load thresholds exist yet. The talk conflicts on wording ("predict" injuries) and offers thresholds without showing their evidence.
- Eric's baseline: daily subjective surveys are kept in return to play. The talk agrees that subjective flags should start a conversation. [30:23]

## What would have to be true

- Enough Baylor football CMJ history (several seasons, consistent protocol) to compute individual and position-group baselines.
- Injury records from Athletic Medicine with dates and mechanism, so non-contact injuries can be separated from contact injuries.
- A sample large enough to see any pattern; one team's single-season injuries are likely too few.
- Evidence, from Baylor data or independent studies, that a flagged phase pattern precedes injury more often than chance. The talk shows none.

## Do not apply when

- Baseball pitcher findings (UCL, drive without load) are carried into football; the speaker says football models are younger. [34:35]
- The vendor's thresholds (t-score 40, difference of 10, drive 15 from others) are used without local data or known units.
- The decision would restrict an athlete based on a single flag with no conversation or medical input.
- The number of injuries is too small to tell a signal from noise.
- The 10 to 20% reduction or savings figures are used to justify spend; the captions do not support them.

## First step

Pull one position group's preseason ForceDecks CMJ data, compute each athlete's own baseline and standard deviation, and list last year's non-contact injuries from Athletic Medicine beside it as a read-only, retrospective look. Change nothing in the current workflow.

---
type: video-summary
video_id: ZNIVzarJwPg
title: "The Performance/Precaution Tradeoff: Player Health"
event: SSAC19 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Gretchen Reynolds (moderator, New York Times columnist), "a dear Schiffman" (caption spelling; executive chairman of Catapult), Dr. John DiFiore (director of sports medicine for the NBA), Casey Smith (head athletic trainer, Dallas Mavericks)]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, basketball, policy, decision-making, other-sport:cricket]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft

## Summary

A panel discusses how wearable, imaging and force data have changed athlete health work over about five years, and where the science still falls short. The panelists say data lets staff quantify where an athlete sits between overtraining and undertraining, argue that too little intensity in practice raises in-game injury risk, and stress individualizing aggregate data. The NBA and its Players Association are running an independent validation process for wearables. Panelists emphasize player trust, the right to see data, asking vendors for research, and lifestyle basics. They admit that return-to-play cutoffs such as 10% symmetry have little risk data behind them. The captions carry no speaker labels, so many claims cannot be tied to one panelist.

## Key claims

- Data on tissue quality, especially tendon structure, changed interventions; tendinopathy was once assumed to be managed, and is now seen as improvable. [03:37] [05:09] [05:39]
- Coaches always knew there is a line beyond which pushing performance risks health; technology now quantifies where athletes sit relative to it. [05:39]
- Protecting athletes too much, such as pulling training back in preseason, does not protect them and raises later injury risk; there is a line at the low end as well. [06:10] [06:40]
- Accumulated history improves individual decisions, and the first three to six months of data make balance hard to get right. [06:40] [07:11]
- Aggregate data helps, but it must be individualized, for example for a player with a prior unstable ankle. [07:42] [08:14]
- A five-year league injury database lets staff avoid overreacting to a few serious injuries. [08:44] [09:15]
- Data gives coaches and medical staff an impetus for change; the conversation should begin with how the player feels, and data are tools for modifiable factors. [09:49] [10:21]
- When a player feels great but markers suggest risk, trust with coaches and ownership on board lets staff dial the player back. [10:51] [11:22]
- Data should be used to extend a career, not only for game-to-game or season-to-season results. [11:53]
- The NBA and the Players Association formed a wearables technology committee and an external validation process with three parts: accuracy and reproducibility, cyber security, and game use. [12:59] [13:32] [14:03] [14:33] [15:04]
- Wearables allow measuring intensity of minutes, rather than relying on minutes played. [15:34]
- Independent validation should stay central, and player health comes before performance or commercial aims. [16:05] [16:35]
- Players control whether data is collected and can see and interpret it; the message is that the data concerns modifiable factors. [17:36] [18:06] [18:38]
- Player availability is described as the most significant factor in an organization's success. [19:09]
- One panelist says the science is solid, independently validated, built over two to three decades; another admits the data may show "this isn't what we thought." [20:41] [21:12] [23:15]
- Teams need a professional who understands data, statistics and sport science, and should use data in aggregate beyond one organization. [21:43] [22:14]
- Many teams and sports are using the technology (about two and a half thousand teams and close to 30 sports), and learnings cross sports. [23:46]
- Combining data streams is a goal; a panelist guesses only about six factors might turn out to matter. [24:16] [25:17]
- A central repository is needed so data is not siloed (a vendor view). [25:47] [26:17]
- Best practices are shared across teams and leagues because player health is league-wide. [26:47] [27:17]
- Evidence-based practice means combining research, clinician experience and the athlete's preference, not applying research directly. [28:48] [29:19]
- Game loads can be replicated in practice; one finding was large amounts of backwards running in basketball. [29:50] [30:21]
- Research is needed that links training load to overall player health, including mental health and illness. [30:53] [31:23] [31:54]
- "Heart" can be described as repeated second efforts: high load under anaerobic conditions. [33:57]
- For youth basketball, the NBA, Junior NBA and USA Basketball built recommendations on age-based practice volume, sleep, rest and sports sampling; early single-sport specialization is not helpful. [35:30] [36:01] [36:32] [37:03]
- Advice needing no technology: do not train or play when hurt; a youth tool focuses on practice load versus game load. [38:04] [38:34]
- Lifestyle, sleep, diet and recovery are the foundation, and staff cannot out-intervene missing basics. [39:36] [40:06]
- Training hard is part of being injury resilient, not injury proof. [40:36]
- Food logs and sleep measurement are used for individual players. [40:36] [41:06]
- Answer new product pitches by asking for research; asking probably wipes out 90% of pitches; anecdote is not sufficient. [43:39] [44:11] [45:12]
- Game-day decisions: explain risk and benefit; if risk is too high, say so. [46:17] [46:47]
- Return to play: when speed and agility look even, force plate and ultrasound data can show remaining deficits, such as deceleration or symmetry. [48:20] [48:51]
- Some practice activities assumed to be easy days were physiologically intense, with heavy acceleration and deceleration in small spaces. [51:26] [51:58]
- In cricket, fast bowlers held back to about 60 to 70% of max speed in practice and were underprepared for games; increasing intensity reduced injuries. A rugby example raised practice contact and reduced game risk. [52:29] [52:59] [53:30]
- Youth biometrics: fine for injury prevention, but fraught if used to drive training or spot talent. [54:02] [55:03]
- The job is neither more art nor more science but a combination. [56:05] [56:37]

## Numbers and definitions

- Panel length: 45 minutes plus about 10 minutes of audience questions. [00:32]
- Time frame: "last five years" [02:06]; working with Casey Smith since 2010 [06:40].
- First three to six months of data: hard to get balance right. [06:40]
- Five-year injury trend window. [08:44]
- Two and a half thousand teams, close to 30 sports. [23:46] The captions may be imprecise; no source is named.
- NBA validation is "only the second league" known to do this. [16:05] Unverified.
- Return-to-play symmetry: "within 10 percent of the uninjured side"; panelists say no aggregate data ties this to a re-entry risk (an example of "2 percent" is hypothetical). [49:54] [50:24]
- Hamstring example: about three-quarters of the way there; waiting another week lowers risk. [46:47] [47:18]
- Cricket: fast bowlers account for 70% of injuries; practice at 60 or 70% of max speed. [52:29] [52:59]
- Asking for research "probably wipes out 90%" of pitches. [45:12]
- ACWR or other load formulas are not named.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Independent validation of wearables: accuracy, reproducibility and comparison of devices across players (Fraunhofer Research Institute in Germany and University of Michigan named). [14:03] [14:33]
- Exposure measured by intensity rather than minutes. [15:34]
- Central data repository combining self-reported, medical, wearable and tactical video data. [26:17]
- Evidence-based practice as research, clinical experience and athlete preference. [28:48]
- Return to play using force plate symmetry, ultrasound and deceleration compared with preseason data. [48:20] [48:51]
- Rating of perceived exertion and other validated psychological tools as part of a "360" approach. [32:26]
- Vendor intake: request the research first. [43:39]

## Limits and open questions

- The captions have no speaker labels. Claims are given to "a panelist"; the panel was moderated and the panelist who said the science is solid is not identified.
- Conflict inside the talk: "science is solid" [21:12] versus no aggregate data linking the 10% symmetry rule to risk [50:24] and "maybe this isn't what we thought" [23:15].
- No sample sizes or study references are given for the tendon, cricket or rugby examples.
- Commercial and institutional views: one panelist represents a wearables vendor (Catapult) and another the league.
- "Only the second league" and "90%" are unsourced.
- Youth guidance is described as broad and "based on data" without detail. [36:01]
- Mental health is raised as a gap with no method given. [31:54]
- Captions misspell names ("Abascal" at [05:09]); Schiffman's name is caption spelling.

## Q&A

- Hardest conversation about playing; did data matter? Explain risk, benefit and the next weeks; retirement decisions are hardest. [45:46] [46:17] [47:18]
- How to change coach and player attitudes toward playing hurt? Risk can be reduced, never zero; objective markers help; coaches have shifted toward science. [48:51] [49:23] [50:55]
- Something unexpected learned from data? Easy days were more intense than expected. [50:55] [51:26]
- Sports outside basketball? Cricket and rugby examples. [52:29] [53:30]
- Will biometrics expand in youth sport? Likely, but use for prevention only. [53:30] [54:02] [55:03]
- Art or science? Both. [56:05]

=== FILE: videos/2019-03-08_ZNIVzarJwPg_the-performance-precaution-tradeoff-player-health/applications.md ===
---
type: video-applications
video_id: ZNIVzarJwPg
status: draft
---

## Where this applies

- Inference: Compare practice intensity and high-speed exposure with game demand in Catapult data for football, to see whether some position groups regularly train well below game peaks (the talk's cricket example of practicing at 60 to 70% of max speed).
- Inference: For hamstring or other lower-limb return to play, put ForceDecks symmetry and deceleration data beside speed and agility results in the conversation with the athlete, using the athlete's own preseason numbers as reference and Athletic Medicine as owner of the decision.
- Inference: Write a vendor-intake step: ask for independent research before any pilot of a new technology, and record the answer.
- Inference: Review "easy day" and walk-through sessions for acceleration and deceleration load, since the talk reports low-key practice often carries more load than staff expect.
- Inference: Give athletes a clear way to see their own data and the reason it is collected, to support buy-in.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: data collection is judged on cost versus insight, and inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data. The talk agrees in asking for validation and reproducibility before use.
- Eric's baseline: recovery has to be earned by training hard, and the field's load-monitoring culture created a "culture of fear" that under-trains athletes. The talk agrees: too little intensity raises game injury risk. [06:10] [52:59]
- Eric's baseline: subjective wellness surveys were dropped for the roster but kept in return to play and chronic health cases. The talk partly extends this: the conversation starts with how the player feels, and subjective input is combined with data. [10:21]
- Eric's baseline: return to play is thin, with no stated criteria. The talk offers a symmetry example and admits the threshold has little risk data. [50:24]
- Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, in collaboration with Athletic Medicine. The talk agrees. [49:23]
- Eric's baseline: a trained "coach's eye" matters as much as technology. The talk agrees with art plus science. [56:05]

## What would have to be true

- Catapult session tags that reliably separate practice types (for example walk-through versus team period) so load can be compared with game peaks.
- Game and practice data from the same devices and thresholds across seasons.
- Preseason ForceDecks baselines for each athlete, collected with the same protocol.
- Agreement with Athletic Medicine on who owns the return-to-play decision and what data is shared.
- A written list of what evidence counts as "independent" for vendors.

## Do not apply when

- NBA, cricket or rugby findings are carried straight into college football without checking Baylor's contact rules and practice limits.
- A symmetry cutoff such as 10% is treated as a proven risk threshold; the panelists say the data are missing.
- Higher practice intensity is added to athletes who are already overloaded or have unresolved injuries.
- Athletes cannot see or question their data, which undercuts the trust the panel describes.
- Fewer than a few seasons of consistent data exist for that position group.

## First step

Write a one-page vendor-intake checklist (research requested, independent validation, reproducibility, data ownership) and use it for the next technology pitch. No data or workflow changes.
